source.title: Scaling convolutional neural networks achieves expert level seizure detection in neonatal EEG
source.authors: Robert Hogan; S. Mathieson; Aurel Luca; S. Ventura; Sean Griffin; G. Boylan; John M. O'Toole

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests model- and data-scaling curves for the same double-descent question using a different CNN, dataset, and application setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own model- and data-scaling results. Results cited from other work are not included. Scaling-curve values are shown in figures, but exact plotted values are not stated in the text; only error-rate results directly bearing on the claim's test-error measure are recorded.
record.test_reason: An applied neonatal-EEG study whose own model-size and data-size sweeps show a non-monotonic dip the authors call deep double descent. It is a new setting (1-D ConvNeXt, EEG seizure detection) rather than a different method aimed at the original question, so T3 fits better than T2. The evidence is five model sizes and figure-only values, with no interpolation-threshold measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors' main conclusions are that scaling data and model size improves neonatal seizure detection and that the XL model reaches expert-level equivalence on two held-out sets. The double-descent dip is reported as an incidental observation in both model and data scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps ConvNeXt width/depth and subsamples neonatal EEG data rather than reproducing the original benchmark settings; it does not measure the interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling trend differs by validation setting: returns diminish for some metrics on Helsinki, and the authors report a different scaling pattern for Helsinki late-EEG versus early-EEG groups (Fig. D2; MCC).
record.problems: Exact error-rate values for the scaling curves are not stated in the text and are only presented in figures. The study does not identify the interpolation threshold, so it cannot establish that the dip occurs near the size at which the model just fits the training set.
record.rows_left_out: Other performance metrics, including MCC and Pearson’s correlation, were not extracted as rows because the claim versions recorded here specify test error. The expert-equivalence results do not bear on the claim.

untested.parts: First descent before the peak; whether the peak lies at the size that just fits the training set (training error not reported).
Whether the data-scaling dip lies near the interpolation threshold.
No test-error curve over epochs is reported; early stopping is discussed only by citation.
Only one architecture family is used.

missing.what: Helsinki subgroup MCC by model size: the early-EEG group reproduces the Small-model dip; the late-EEG group peaks at Medium and degrades for Large/XL.
MCC/Pearson r dip at Small in model scaling, which is the metric the authors emphasise; the error-rate rows alone may not capture it.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent is a side observation in an applied paper. Evidence rests on five model sizes, figure-only values, no training-error or interpolation measurement, and apparently single runs for model scaling. The Helsinki degradation is attributed by the authors to distribution shift, not to double descent.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure where models just fit the training set or establish that the dip is near an interpolation threshold.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The study reports a data-scaling dip but does not locate it relative to an interpolation threshold.
Only one CNN model family is studied; the claim across model classes is not tested.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not test noise dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter measure.

rows.subject: ConvNeXt model variants (Nano, Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large; aggregate sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size by changing network width and depth; evaluated the development test set.

conditions.value: Nano, Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large

rows.note: The text says performance dips for Small relative to Nano and recovers at larger sizes; the figure includes error rate among its metrics. Exact error-rate values are not stated.
rows.check: Only the rise-then-fall part is visible: Small (289.2k) is worse than Nano (38.7k), then Medium to XL recover. With five sizes there is no initial descent and no evidence the peak sits near the interpolation threshold. It appears to be a single run per size (error bars are stated only for Fig. 2a). The text says the dip shows in 'all metrics', which includes error rate, but values are figure-only.

rows.subject: Medium ConvNeXt
rows.operation_detail: Subsampled the training dataset by annotated EEG hours while keeping the Medium model fixed.

conditions.value: 1 k to 10 k hours of EEG

rows.uncertainty: min/max over 3 trials; values figure only
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe a performance decrease as data increases from 1 k to 10 k hours, followed by improvement with further data. The figure includes error rate, but exact values are not stated.
rows.check: The authors describe only 'some evidence' of a decrease from 1k to 10k hours, within min/max error bars over 3 trials. The metric showing it is not specified, and the dip is not located relative to an interpolation threshold.

source_check.correct: For error rate specifically, state=cannot_determine from the supplied text. Figure 2a error bars represent min/max over 3 trials.
